families.s: HSE working-under-vehicles support, lifting and examination guidance
families.t: vehicle support, jacks, stands, chocking, lift installation, balance, inspection, examination and competence
f: Vehicles falling or rolling from incorrectly positioned jacks or stands are a leading cause of fatal motor-repair incidents.
A vehicle must be supported by equipment of adequate capacity and stability before anyone works beneath it.
Wheels should be chocked where movement could occur, and jacks should not be treated as the sole support.
Lift floors, fixings and installation must meet the manufacturer's requirements and be tested before use.
Vehicle balance and centre-of-gravity changes must be considered when heavy components are removed.
Two-post lift arm locks and lifting-pad positions should be checked before full elevation.
Vehicle lifts require regular in-house checks, maintenance and periodic thorough examination by a competent person.
Work away from the workshop needs the same secure-support principles and should avoid improvised or unstable supports.
families.g: Working-under-vehicle risk depends on vehicle mass and balance, support equipment and ground, positioning and chocking, lift installation, maintenance, examination, task forces and competence.

families.s: HSE two-post vehicle-lift arm-locking and stability guidance
families.t: arm locks, lifting pads, rated capacity, vehicle lifting points, weight distribution, short test lift, installation and daily checks
f: Two-post lifts without effective arm-locking systems should not remain in use.
Arm-locking mechanisms and support-arm rubber mounts should be checked daily.
All controls should operate correctly before the lift is used.
The manufacturer's rated capacity and vehicle-size limitations must be followed.
Correct manufacturer-specified jacking or lifting points should be identified for each vehicle.
The effect of removing engines, gearboxes or other heavy parts on vehicle stability must be assessed.
A vehicle should first be raised a short distance so arm locks and pad positions can be checked.
Lift installers must be competent and the supporting floor must have adequate strength.
families.g: Two-post-lift risk depends on lift design and condition, arm locks and pads, vehicle geometry and load distribution, installation and floor, operator checks, task forces and maintenance.

families.s: HSE vehicle air-suspension collapse and stored-energy control guidance
families.t: air suspension, chassis lowering, stored pressure, deflation, props, stands, roadside work, component release and repair facilities
f: Serious air-suspension incidents have involved inadequately supported vehicles and unintended component rupture or release.
Air suspension must never be relied on to maintain ride height while a person is in a trapping zone.
Suspension movement should be prevented by deflating the system or using suitably rated props or stands.
Support points and equipment should be compatible with the particular vehicle and repair task.
Stored pressure should be controlled before components, pipework or bellows are disturbed.
Roadside or third-party-site repair should be kept to the minimum necessary.
Where practicable, air-suspension repairs should be moved to an adequately equipped repair facility.
Roadside systems of work must also protect vehicle occupants, workers and other road users.
families.g: Air-suspension risk depends on vehicle design and ride height, stored pressure, support and deflation method, access and trapping zones, location, component condition and competence.

families.s: HSE tyre removal, replacement and inflation stored-energy guidance
families.t: competence, inspection, stored energy, trajectory zone, airline length, restraints, pressure control, large tyres and damaged tyres
f: Tyre removal, replacement and inflation should only be carried out by competent staff.
Manual handling and hand-tool injuries are common in tyre work and must be included in the assessment.
An inflated tyre stores substantial energy and a failure can release explosive force.
The operator should stand outside the likely failure trajectory during inflation.
The airline between the clip-on chuck and control should be long enough for safe positioning.
Higher-pressure light-commercial, truck and bus tyres may require a suitable restraint or cage.
Pressure gauges, regulators and inflation equipment should prevent uncontrolled overpressure.
Very large tyres require a planned system that restrains the wheel, controls blast effects and keeps everyone outside the trajectory.
families.g: Tyre-inflation risk depends on tyre and wheel construction, size and pressure, condition and damage, restraint and airline arrangement, operator position, equipment calibration and competence.

families.s: HSE multipiece and split-wheel deflation, inspection and reinflation guidance
families.t: multipiece wheels, split rims, flange rings, deflation, visual inspection, 15 psi seating check, cage, airline, repairs and specialist competence
f: Multipiece-wheel explosions can occur during reinflation, refitting, deflation or wheel removal.
Fitters must recognise different wheel constructions and understand their specific hazards.
Best practice is to deflate pneumatic tyres before removing multipiece wheels.
Where flange components cannot be fully inspected, deflation should be required before removal.
Safety-critical defects require the wheel or tyre assembly to be withdrawn from use.
Wheel components should not be repaired in ways that could impair assembly strength or integrity.
Initial reinflation should be limited to about 15 psi while bead and loose-component seating is checked.
Higher inflation should use pressure control, a long airline and a purpose-built enclosure or other suitable restraint.
families.g: Multipiece-wheel risk depends on construction and component seating, tyre pressure and condition, visibility, deflation and restraint, repair history, inflation equipment and specialist competence.
